subject: Incorporating Imputation into MethylKit's analysis pipeline

messages.author: 709128a5e618771e
messages.subject: Incorporating Imputation into MethylKit's analysis pipeline
parts:
Hi,

I was wondering if MethylKit is capable of analysing lower-depth WGBS datasets that have had any missing methylation values imputed? 

I've experimented with using MethIMPUTE, which produces a methylation level for missing values - but the unite() function produces an object that uses coverage values, which would remain as 0 for imputed values, whereas the methylation value would be changed. 

Does anyone use imputation in their analysis with MethylKit? And if so, what is your recommended best practice in incorporating it into your analysis pipeline?

Best,

Dean

messages.author: ab8277113f65c05e
messages.subject: Re: [methylkit_discussion] Incorporating Imputation into MethylKit's analysis pipeline
parts:
This can be done but needs a bit of work. If you use k-nearest neighbor method for imputation you can use methylation ratios to calculate k-nearest neighbors then use the same neighbors to calculate coverage value as mean of coverage values from nearest neighbors, rounded to the nearest integer. Then you can work out number of Cs and Ts from the imputed methylation ratio.

How many samples do you have ? Is this single-cell data? 

Best
Altuna

Hi, 

Thanks for the speedy reply! Hopefully I can get those steps to work.

It is not single cell, but WGBS of tumour samples. My dataset size is currently 10, but will be working with more (~40) once I've ironed out the pipeline.

Im wanting to observe the effects that lower coverage has on sample correlation, DMR detection, as well as the capability of the data to be clustered/subgrouped. 

The goal is to determine the lowest adequate level of coverage (and subsequently costs) that can be used to subgroup a new cohort of samples.

Dean
